# Allama Ghulam Ali Okarvi (1919–2000)

Allama Ghulam Ali Okarvi was a renowned Pakistani Islamic scholar, orator, and religious leader associated with the Barelvi movement of Sunni Islam. He was widely regarded as one of the most influential Sunni orators of the 20th century in the Indian subcontinent.

## Early Life and Background
- **Born:** 1919 in Mubarakpur, Azamgarh district, Uttar Pradesh, British India
- His family later relocated, and he became associated with the town of **Okara** in Punjab, Pakistan, from which his nisbah "Okarvi" is derived
- He migrated to Pakistan after the partition in 1947

## Education
He studied under several prominent scholars of his era and received traditional Islamic education in subjects including:
- Tafsir (Quranic exegesis)
- Hadith
- Fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence)
- Arabic literature and logic

He was a student/khalifa associated with the Razavi/Barelvi tradition founded by Imam Ahmed Raza Khan.

## Contributions and Work
- **Orator:** He was famously known as "Khateeb-e-Azam" (The Great Orator) of Pakistan due to his powerful speaking style
- **Author:** Wrote numerous books on Islamic theology, the life of Prophet Muhammad (Seerah), and refutations of opposing theological positions
- His lectures (often delivered during Rabi-ul-Awwal milad gatherings) were widely circulated on cassettes and later digital media
- He defended traditional Sunni Barelvi positions on issues like Milad-un-Nabi, visiting graves of saints, and intercession

## Notable Works
Some of his well-known writings include works on:
- Seerah of the Prophet Muhammad
- Defenses of Sunni Barelvi beliefs
- Polemical works against the Deobandi and Wahhabi/Salafi positions

## Legacy
- His son, **Maulana Kaukab Noorani Okarvi**, continued his work and is also a prominent Sunni Barelvi scholar and orator
- The Okarvi family established institutions and continues to promote his teachings
- His recorded speeches remain popular among Barelvi Muslims worldwide

## Death
He passed away in 2000.
